papers.title: Pooled sequencing reveals patterns of underlying genomic divergence in Drosophila chronotypes
papers.abstract: Chronotypes, often referred to in the context of sleep timing in humans (early/late sleepers) are heritable variations in timing of circadian behaviours. Chronotype differences among individuals have been associated with a myriad of psychological, metabolic, and physiological dysregulations. Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) in humans have identified several circadian clock gene polymorphisms associated with divergent chronotypes; however, the lists of candidate genes vary across studies based on methodology and sampling strategy thus, necessitating more controlled studies on well-established model systems. Using long-term experimental evolution approach spanning over 20 years, we have derived a unique set of chronotypes in the form of 12 replicate Drosophila melanogaster populations that exhibit early/morning and late/evening emergence and have previously reported several circadian clock differences between the populations. We performed pooled DNA sequencing to explore genomic differences underlying early and late chronotypes and identified multiple genomic regions under selection. We observe that the early chronotype populations have primarily accumulated polymorphisms in genes related to photosensitivity, sleep, and the circadian clock, while the late chronotype populations have largely accumulated polymorphisms in genes related to the circadian clock, mRNA splicing mechanisms, and ecdysis. We further predict biological pathways under differential selection in the early and late chronotype populations. We believe these results provide evolutionary mechanisms behind chronotype divergence and will help generate verifiable hypothesis regarding target genes for phase divergence.

papers.title: Extensive HGT between soil-living hexapods contributes to functional convergence
papers.abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has been documented in diverse metazoan lineages, with most reported cases involving putative non-metazoan donors. Here, we combine protein taxonomic assignment with distance-based and phylogenetic approaches to infer 440 independent HGT events in sciarid flies (Sciaridae, Diptera). While 67 of these events involve genes of non-metazoan origin (mainly from bacteria and fungi), 352 likely occurred directly between sciarid flies and another group of soil-dwelling hexapods, the springtails (Collembola). Most of these HGTs (n=264) occurred in the springtail-to-sciarid orientation and involve genes that are expressed, evolve under functional constraints, and are enriched in carbohydrate and redox metabolism. Remarkably, genes springtails acquired independently from non-metazoans are enriched in the same functional categories. Consistent with the proposed role of these genes in processing plant- and fungal-derived polysaccharides and lignin compounds, their expression in a sciarid species is particularly high in larvae, which, like springtails, graze on plant and fungal resources. Because springtails were present in terrestrial habitats long before sciarid flies, our results suggest sciarid colonization of these habitats may have been facilitated by the horizontal acquisition of numerous springtail genes that were useful in soil and functional in a metazoan background. They also reveal that metazoan-to-metazoan HGT can be common in some lineages, calling for an in-depth investigation of the mechanisms underlying these transfers and for a systematic appraisal of their consequences on metazoan evolution.

papers.title: Inactivation of prenyltransferase inhibitors by S-methylation catalyzed by the methyltransferases TMT1A (METTL7A) and TMT1B (METTL7B)
papers.abstract: The thiol methyltransferases TMT1A and TMT1B (formerly METTL7A and METTL7B) metabolize thiol-containing compounds, but their substrate range and effects on drug activity remain incompletely defined. Here, we investigated whether these enzymes methylate protein prenyltransferase inhibitors and alter cellular sensitivity to these compounds. Mass spectrometry identified several thiol-containing farnesyltransferase and geranylgeranyltransferase inhibitors as substrates of both enzymes, whereas other thiol-containing inhibitors showed no detectable methylation. In HT1080 fibrosarcoma cells, TMT1A or TMT1B overexpression conferred resistance to several geranylgeranyltransferase inhibitors and attenuated drug-induced cell-cycle arrest. Pharmacological inhibition of TMT1A with 2,3-Dichloro--methylbenzylamine (DCMB, LY-78335) reversed resistance and restored cell-cycle arrest in TMT1A-expressing cells. These findings expand the known substrate range of TMT1A and TMT1B and support TMT-dependent methylation as a mechanism that reduces the cellular activity of susceptible prenyltransferase inhibitors.

papers.title: Extracellular Lactate Inhibits HIV Infection in Dendritic Cells by Downregulating CD4 Expression
papers.abstract: Cellular metabolism and cellular microenvironments influences immune-cell function. We previously demonstrated that interleukin-27 (IL-27)-induced monocyte-derived dendritic cells (27DCs) exhibit resistance to HIV-1. A mechanistic study for this antiviral effect suggested that in addition to inducing antiviral genes, IL-27 may influence cellular metabolism that contributes to the anti-HIV effect. During course of study, we observed that 27DCs accumulated lactate in culture supernatants by 5.7-fold increase compared with cultures of untreated DCs (iDCs) (12.1{+/-}1.3 versus 2.1{+/-}0.2 mM). Here, we assesses extracellular role of lactate on HIV infection. Healthy donors CD14+ monocytes were differentiated to DCs using GM-CSF and IL-4 in the absence of presence of lactate (Lac). DCs were infected with HIVAD8. Lactate-induced DC (LacDC) reduced R5-tropic HIV-1 AD8 replication by 71.1{+/-}8.3% without detectable cytotoxicity compared to that in untreated cells (iDCs). LacDCs exhibited reductions in viral particles binding, membrane fusion of viral particles, and HIV reverse-transcription by 78.5{+/-}2.8% (n=3, p<0.05), 78.7{+/-}3.3% (n=3, p<0.01), 86.2{+/-}5.7% (n=3. p<0.01), respectively. FACS analyses demonstrated that surface CD4 expression on LacDC decreased by 56.6{+/-}5.1% (n=5 , p<0.05) compared to iDC, whereas total cellular CD4 protein amount and surface CCR5 expression were not significantly altered. Neither the lactate transporter inhibitor nor the lactate receptor restored HIV-1 susceptibility. These findings demonstrate that lactate exposure during dendritic-cell differentiation induces an HIV-1-resistant phenotype associated with reduced surface CD4 availability and impaired viral attachment. This study identifies extracellular lactate as a modulator of dendritic-cell susceptibility to HIV-1 and suggests a potential link between IL-27-associated metabolic changes and antiviral immunity.

papers.title: Extensive SARS-CoV-2 spike sequence diversification converges on a bounded, low-dimensional physicochemical space
papers.abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, SARS-CoV-2 accumulated extensive amino acid variation in its spike protein. However, the extent to which sequence diversification translates into physicochemical diversity remains unclear. Here, we analyzed 271,769 unique spike protein sequences from 12 geographical regions using three physicochemical descriptors: net charge at pH 7.0, hydropathy, and aliphatic index. To characterize temporal changes in physicochemical space, we compared the squared Mahalanobis distances of observed sequences with those of Monte Carlo-simulated sequences containing randomized amino acid substitutions, constrained to the number of empirically variable positions. We applied trimmed clustering to characterize sequence distributions in physicochemical space and used Shannon entropy to assess spatiotemporal relationships between genotypic and physicochemical diversity across geographic regions. Empirical physicochemical displacement increased early in the observation period and subsequently stabilized, despite continued increases in variable amino acid positions and accumulated substitutions. In contrast, simulated trajectories exhibited greater and sustained physicochemical divergence. Trimmed clustering identified six distinct physicochemical groups repeatedly occupied by genetically divergent lineages differing in mutation burden, amino acid composition, and emergence time. Shannon entropy analyses revealed broadly similar nonlinear temporal patterns across geographic regions, with differences between genotypic and physicochemical entropy tending to be negative. These findings indicate that extensive spike protein sequence diversification occurred within a comparatively restricted physicochemical space, consistent with a many-to-one relationship between amino acid sequences and physicochemical states. This framework provides a quantitative approach for investigating physicochemical constraints on viral protein evolution and may inform future machine learning approaches to epitope prediction and vaccine antigen design.

papers.title: Mapping the genetic landscape of cell morphogenesis and subcellular organization in stationary-phase Escherichia coli cells
papers.abstract: In nature, many bacteria reside in a non-growing stationary phase. The extent and genetic basis of the accompanying cellular remodeling remain unclear. Here, we developed Coli-Painting, a combinatorial staining assay, and BactoScoop, a dedicated image-based profiling pipeline, to characterize the growth-to-stasis transition in Escherichia coli. Single-cell profiles revealed a gradual yet heterogeneous entry, with some cells retaining signs of chromosome replication or cell division well into stationary phase. Subsequent genome-wide profiling identified genetic determinants of stationary-phase cell morphology, nucleoid organization, RNA distribution, and membrane-related properties. Global correlations among cellular features revealed coordinated aspects of stationary-phase cell architecture, while high-dimensional mutant profiles provided functional context for genes of known and unknown function. Downstream characterization of 19 y-genes highlighted the ability of our approach to identify relevant contributors to stationary-phase physiology. Overall, our work uncovers the genetic landscape of stationary-phase cell organization in E. coli and serves as a resource for uncovering growth-stage-specific gene function.

papers.title: Flux analysis resolves distinct brain uptake and clearance of TfR- and CD98hc-targeting large molecules
papers.abstract: Advances in large-molecule delivery across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) by targeting receptors such as transferrin receptor (TfR) or CD98 heavy chain (CD98hc) are shifting the focus from restricted parenchymal access toward brain exposure profiles tailored to therapeutic needs. However, brain concentrations offer only partial insight into delivery mechanisms, as they reflect the net balance of two dynamic processes: flux of molecules entering and leaving the brain, here termed brain uptake and brain clearance, respectively. Here, we establish a generalizable experimental and mathematical modeling framework to resolve these opposing fluxes and demonstrate its application using pharmacokinetic (PK) data from Fc-engineered antibody transport vehicles (ATVs) targeting TfR or CD98hc in humanized knock-in mouse models. First, to directly estimate brain clearance, we engineered anti-ATV antibodies that selectively bind the TV patch to block receptor-mediated brain uptake in vivo. Integrating these measurements with a mechanistic PK model, we then reconstructed brain fluxes of ATV molecules over time across a broad range of receptor affinities. Results demonstrated that TfR-targeting promotes rapid, affinity-dependent brain uptake accompanied by comparatively rapid brain clearance, whereas CD98hc-targeting results in slower brain uptake and prolonged retention. Extending this framework to dual TfR/CD98hc-targeting ATVs suggested that higher observed brain exposure relative to single-receptor formats does not necessarily translate to greater brain delivery: increased exposure was predicted to arise primarily from reduced brain clearance, associated with CD98hc-mediated retention, rather than enhanced uptake through dual-receptor engagement. Together, these results establish a quantitative basis for resolving brain fluxes and engineering brain-targeted biologics for desired therapeutic outcomes.

papers.title: Male host suppressors mask Wolbachia-induced cytoplasmic incompatibility in the invasive pest Drosophila suzukii
papers.abstract: Cytoplasmic incompatibility (CI) is the most widespread reproductive manipulation induced by the endosymbiotic bacteria Wolbachia in arthropods. When infected males mate with uninfected females, some or all embryos die, which favors infected females and drives the spread of the symbiont through host populations. The Wolbachia cif genes that cause CI have been identified, but they do not explain why CI strength varies among host genotypes. The invasive fruit pest Drosophila suzukii illustrates a related paradox: its Wolbachia strain wSuz carries cif genes, yet CI has not been detected in this host species. Combining experimental crosses with genomic and cytological approaches, we show that wSuz does induce CI, with paternal chromosomes showing segregation defects during the first zygotic division. However, CI strength ranges from undetectable to 67% among males from four European host lines. This variation was explained neither by Wolbachia titer in testes nor by the Wolbachia genome, which was nearly identical among isolates and invariant at cif loci. Instead, CI strength depended on the genotype of infected males, whereas the genotype of uninfected females had no detectable effect. Reciprocal F1 and F2 crosses revealed that CI is masked by partially dominant autosomal host suppressors, probably involving a few loci. Masking by host suppressors thus explains the apparent absence of CI in D. suzukii, and host suppressors of CI may also shape the efficacy and evolutionary success of Wolbachia-based pest and vector control strategies.

papers.title: KDM3B enforces a non-mutational ErbB signaling state that sustains cholangiocarcinoma
papers.abstract: More than 50% of cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) patients lack druggable mutations, showing broad non-mutational epigenetic perturbations, whose mechanistic insights and clinical benefit remain largely unexplored. Across multiple CCA patient cohorts, we identified prevalent significant upregulation of lysine demethylase (KDM) gene families, with KDM3B emerging as a critical epigenetic dependency for sustaining tumor fitness. KDM3B loss reduced colony formation, proliferation, and migration across intra- and extrahepatic CCA tumor models. Integrated multi-omics linked KDM3B to ErbB activation and downstream PI3K-AKT oncogenic signaling. Mechanistically, KDM3B is bound to the ERBB3 promoter, removing repressive H3K9me2 marks to transcriptionally activate ERBB3, augmenting ErbB receptor activity. Spatial and single cell transcriptomics from patient tumors revealed that high KDM3B-ERBB3 coupling reshapes the tumor niche via enhancing the epithelial-mesenchymal transition crosstalk with neighborhood cells to establish a pro-invasive microenvironment. Pharmacologic inhibition in vivo of the KDM3B downstream ERBB-Akt regulatory axis suppressed CCA xenograft tumor growth. These findings establish KDM3B as a non-mutational epigenetic activator of ErbB-driven signaling, reshaping the tumor ecosystem, and defining the KDM3B-ErbB axis as a vulnerability in CCA.

papers.title: Spindle minus-end microtubule protrusions perturb force balance and delay chromosome segregation
papers.abstract: Mitotic spindle function depends on multiple forces that are difficult to measure in cells. In fission yeast, the spindle assembles and elongates within an intact nuclear envelope. Without the kinesin-14/Pkl1, spindle microtubule minus ends detach from the spindle pole body and are pushed beyond it by kinesin-5/Cut7 sliding, forming protrusions that deform the nuclear envelope. We quantified and modeled protrusion dynamics. We found that as protrusions grew, the spindle often shortened, and the extent of shortening correlated with loss of spindle Cut7. Cells with protrusions showed a delay in anaphase onset. A force-balance model can explain fast and slow protrusion length changes, and inferred overlap length at force balance estimated the midzone sliding force density. After laser ablation, severed protrusions retracted and stopped near the cut, consistent with nuclear envelope-driven sliding. The results show the importance of minus-end anchoring for spindle mechanics and how protrusions can probe mechanical coupling between the spindle and nuclear envelope.

papers.title: TIP60/KAT5-mediated regulation of apoptotic sensitivity during DNA damage-induced senescence
papers.abstract: Cellular senescence and apoptosis are two distinct outcomes to DNA damage. It is unclear what determines the fate decision and the characteristics of senescent cells. Chromatin modifiers are likely candidates, as they can influence the environment for repair of DNA double-strand breaks as well as the transcription of senescent genes. Here we report that the lysine acetyltransferase TIP60/KAT5 is a dosage-sensitive determinant of senescent cell identity in normal human fibroblasts. Although TIP60 is not required for the senescence-associated proliferation arrest of cells after a single dose of 10 Gy of ionising radiation, the resolution of 53BP1 and {gamma}H2AX foci as well as the amplitude of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) as measured by transcript and protein levels of secreted factors is dependent on the levels of TIP60. Furthermore, the sensitivity of senescent cells to apoptosis is also modulated by TIP60 levels. Cells with low levels of TIP60 show reduced p53 output and high levels of the anti-apoptotic protein MCL-1 and are completely resistant to the senolytic ABT-263. Cells with high levels of TIP60 are modestly more sensitive to ABT-263. These results place TIP60 upstream of the divergence of senescent phenotypes and establish that proliferation arrest and the SASP are uncoupled by the level of a single chromatin modifier. We further identify TIP60 as a candidate determinant of senolytic / senomorphic response and suggest that MCL-1 co-inhibition could be used as a rational addition in contexts where TIP60 levels are low.

papers.title: DNA and H3K4 methylation act cooperatively to protect regulatory elements
papers.abstract: Histone H3 lysine 4 methylation (H3K4me) is associated with transcriptionally active regulatory elements: H3K4me1 is typically found at enhancers, and H3K4me2/3 at gene promoters. In mammals, the presence of H3K4me can reinforce expression programs, but it might also help protect from epigenetic silencing complexes. To wit, H3K4me antagonizes the binding of the de novo DNA methyltransferase enzymes, which catalyze the repressive 5-methylcytosine (5meC) epigenetic mark. To determine the extent to which H3K4me protects regulatory elements from 5meC deposition - and how this influences genome regulation - we used mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs), which are resilient to the complete absence of 5meC. Employing an inducible dominant negative transgene that globally reduces H3K4me, we assessed the impact in both presence and absence of 5meC. Surprisingly, while ESCs could withstand reduced H3K4me or 5meC, their combined loss led to catastrophic cellular phenotypes in pluripotency and during differentiation. Genomic analyses revealed that H3K4me and 5meC work in concert to protect regulatory elements from Polycomb-mediated silencing. Thus, this work unraveled an unexpected functional cooperation between two epigenetic marks typically viewed as antagonistic in safeguarding transcriptional programs.

papers.title: An HWE/HisKA2-family kinase-phosphatase pair differentially regulates two paralogous PhyR response regulators to shape the General Stress Response specificity in Sphingopyxis granuli TFA
papers.abstract: The general stress response (GSR) enables bacteria to withstand diverse environmental challenges. In Alphaproteobacteria, the GSR is controlled by a partner-switching mechanism involving the extracytoplasmic function sigma factor EcfG, its anti-sigma factor NepR, and the response regulator PhyR. Phosphorylated PhyR binds to NepR, releasing EcfG to activate GSR gene expression. However, how upstream signalling coordinates multiple PhyR paralogs remains poorly understood. Sphingopyxis granuli TFA is a pollutant-degrading bacterium able to use the organic solvent tetralin as a sole carbon and energy source. TFA contains two copies of each core GSR regulatory component, including two PhyR paralogs with distinct contributions to GSR activity and stress resistance. Using genetic, physiological and biochemical approaches, we identify two HWE/HisKA2-family proteins, HK_3483 and HK_1165, as major positive and negative GSR regulators, respectively. HK_3483 functions as a histidine kinase required for effective GSR activation through either PhyR paralog and for resistance to oxidative stress, copper and desiccation. It directly phosphorylates both PhyR proteins in vitro, with a preference for PhyR1. In contrast, HK_1165 preferentially dephosphorylates PhyR2. Consistently, deletion of SGRAN_1165 in a {Delta}phyR1 background increases PhyR2 phosphorylation in vivo under oxidative stress and stationary phase. Loss of HK_1165 causes a pronounced growth defect that is suppressed by deletion of either PhyR paralog while the remaining PhyR paralog supports elevated GSR activity and broad stress resistance. Our findings support a model in which differential regulation of PhyR phosphorylation, mediated by the opposing activities of an upstream kinase-phosphatase pair, contributes to functional specialization within bacterial stress signalling networks.

papers.title: Multi-omic longitudinal profiling of companion dogs reveals cross-omic coordination and structured aging trajectories
papers.abstract: Aging is a systems-level biological process shaped by coordinated changes across molecular, physiological, and environmental domains, yet how these domains interact and impact aging remains poorly understood. Companion dogs offer a powerful model for addressing this gap, combining shared human environments with diversity in genetics, lifespan, and disease susceptibility. Here, we present a longitudinal multi-omic analysis of aging in 965 companion dogs from the Dog Aging Project, integrating microbiome, epigenome, blood metabolome, and immune phenotyping with extensive clinical, environmental, and lifestyle surveys. We reveal an interconnected cross-omic architecture, with age emerging as the dominant axis of biological variation. We further identify a predictive multi-omic aging signature, distinguish linear from non-linear aging trajectories, uncover breed size-dependent dynamics, and characterize omic-specific mortality risk. Collectively, our findings reveal organizing principles of aging, many paralleling human observations, provide a unique resource for integrative geroscience, and establish dogs as a translational model for aging research.

papers.title: Sisyphus at the splenic flexure: sidedness in colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer is divided into left and right to guide prognosis and therapy, yet a precise definition of left vs right sided colorectal cancer is still not fully agreed upon. The published conventions place it anywhere between the cecum and the rectosigmoid junction. The dichotomy assumes side homogeneity, i.e., that colorectal subsites within a side add limited information once the side is known. That assumption has been examined primarily through mutation prevalence, a quantity that confounds how often a driver arises with how strongly it is selected once it has. Analyzing 1,027 whole-exome and whole-genome sequenced colorectal tumors, we decomposed the prevalence of six driver groups into mutation supply and cancer effect, and asked whether a binary side label captures how each of their prevalence, mutation supply, and cancer effect vary along the colorectum. Mostly it does: the mutational input behaves as two blocks, and even the more than thirty-fold strengthening of cancer effect on BRAF V600E from sigmoid colon to cecum is adequately captured by side. But APC shows nominal evidence against side homogeneity in both prevalence and cancer effect while showing little net left-right difference, and PIK3CA H1047 rejects it in supply. The evidence for finer resolution is real but partial, and the failures do not announce themselves. We recommend additional research recording primary tumor location at the finest practicable resolution--at minimum, International Classification of Diseases for Oncology, 3rd Edition (ICD-O-3) topography. Such well-annotated datasets would enable the left-right boundary to be a reversible analytic choice rather than an irreversible annotation.

papers.title: Beyond tortoises and hares: Niche lability and a continuum of diversification dynamics underlie the megadiversity of a legume genus
papers.abstract: [bullet] Variation in macroevolutionary dynamics, from rapid radiations to slower evolutionary change, can shape multiple facets of biodiversity. However, whether the contributions of contrasting macroevolutionary dynamics to biodiversity differ across timescales, and whether shifts in abiotic niches drive recent radiations, remain open questions in evolutionary biology. [bullet] Using the megadiverse genus Mimosa, we investigate the contribution of contrasting macroevolutionary dynamics to biodiversity and what drives these dynamics at shallow timescales. We combined species-diversity, morphological, and abiotic niche data to estimate biodiversity metrics, infer macroevolutionary rates, and test the role of abiotic niche lability as a driver of radiation-like dynamics. [bullet] We found that Mimosa clades are distributed across a continuum of macroevolutionary dynamics, with those clades resembling radiations clearly contributing to most diversity and disparity, but not niche breadth. Moreover, rates of altitudinal and edaphic niche change were associated with diversification, whereas rates of change in these two niche dimensions, along with climatic niche change, were associated with morphological evolution. Finally, the contribution of radiations to biodiversity seemed to decrease toward the present. [bullet] Overall, our work highlights that both relatively rapid and slow lineage diversification underlie the multifaceted nature of biodiversity and reinforces the role of abiotic niche lability in plant diversification.

papers.title: Characterization and Evaluation of Hypoxia and LPS Preconditioned Placental Stem Cell Extracellular Vesicles in Immune and Intestinal Cells
papers.abstract: Background: Human placental stem cells (hPSCs) have demonstrated therapeutic potential in experimental necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). Extracellular vesicles (EVs) secreted by the hPSCs contribute to these effects through paracrine signaling, however the molecular composition and biological activity of EVs can be influenced by culture conditions of the hPSCs. This study investigated whether hypoxic or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) preconditioning of the hPSCs alters the characteristics, protein composition, and biological activity of hPSC-derived EVs. Methods: hPSCs were cultured under normoxic conditions, exposed to hypoxia (5% O2), or preconditioned with LPS (50 {micro}g/mL). EVs were isolated from conditioned medium using ultrafiltration and size-exclusion chromatography, followed by characterized via nanoparticle tracking analysis, transmission electron microscopy, and single-particle detection of CD9, CD63, and CD81. Biological activity was evaluated in HIEC-6 intestinal epithelial cells through MTT, scratch wound closure, and nitrite detection assays. Immunomodulatory responses were examined in primary healthy neonatal rat CD4+ T-cell cultures using flow cytometry. Results: EV preparations showed comparable particle concentrations and size distributions across all three culture conditions, with no statistically significant differences. Vesicle-like morphology and EV-associated tetraspanins were detected in all preparations. All three EV groups improved epithelial metabolic activity following LPS exposure, enhanced scratch wound closure, and reduced nitrite accumulation compared with their respective controls. Flow cytometric analysis showed no statistically significant differences in TNF-, IL-17A, or FoxP3 expression among EV-treated CD4+ T-cell groups. Conclusions: Hypoxic and LPS preconditioning did not significantly affect the measured physical characteristics or secretion concentrations of the EVs. Although EVs from all three conditions showed beneficial effects on intestinal epithelial cells, neither preconditioning approach demonstrated a clear functional advantage over naive EVs in these simplified culture model. These findings suggest that preconditioning influences EV molecular cargo but more comprehensive biological function assays are required to delineate potential differences in effects on intestinal epithelial or T-cell functions. These data provide a basis for further studies examining its potential relevance to EV-based therapies for NEC.

papers.title: B-RANKO: An ncRNA Foundation Model with Bidirectional Decoder-Only Architecture
papers.abstract: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) plays central roles in gene expression, regulation and catalysis, and has emerged as an important target for therapeutic design. While recent RNA foundation models have achieved strong performance on representation learning tasks, relatively few approaches support both native sequence generation and transferable representation learning within a single framework. We present B-RANKO, a 150M-parameter bidirectional decoder-only ncRNA foundation model that introduces a novel bidirectional autoregressive attention mechanism, enabling a single architecture to support both de novo sequence generation and representation learning. Pretrained on a large corpus derived from RNAcentral, Rfam and GARNET, B-RANKO generates biologically plausible and thermodynamically realistic RNA sequences that exhibit strong novelty relative to their closest matches in the pretraining corpus. We further show that B-RANKO can be efficiently fine-tuned for aptamer generation and achieves competitive performance on BEACON, with particularly strong results on RNA engineering tasks. B-RANKO is publicly available on GitHub at filipvucenik/B-RANKO, together with usage examples and instructions for downloading model weights and datasets.

papers.title: Dog shelter facilitated transmission and maintenance of benzimidazole resistance-associated alleles in canine hookworms
papers.abstract: Anthelmintic resistance in canine hookworms is increasingly recognised; however, environmental settings that maintain and disseminate resistance-associated alleles remain poorly defined. We hypothesised that urban dog shelters act as hotspots for transmission of benzimidazole resistance-associated alleles in Ancylostoma caninum. Residual faecal samples (n=173) were collected from a Sydney, Australia metropolitan shelter over four sampling periods and analysed using coprodiagnostic methods and deep amplicon sequencing targeting ITS-2 and isotype-1 {beta}-tubulin loci. Hookworm eggs were detected in 41% of samples, with A. caninum identified in 97% of sequenced infections and U. stenocephala in 8%. The isotype-1 {beta}-tubulin F167Y mutation was detected in 83% of A. caninum-positive samples, although high allele frequencies (>70%) were uncommon. Longitudinal sampling identified ten dogs that acquired A. caninum during shelter residence, nine of which acquired populations carrying the F167Y mutation. These findings support the role of dog shelters as hotspots for maintenance and dissemination of benzimidazole resistance-associated alleles in canine hookworms. While the impact of this dissemination remains uncertain, ongoing surveillance and targeted anthelmintic stewardship are likely to be important in high-density dog populations.

papers.title: Cabbage1 and Cabbage2 encode CYP90A orthologs that function redundantly to regulate plant development in maize
papers.abstract: Ideal plant architecture improves grain yield per unit area in maize fields by promoting upright leaves which support high planting densities, improving light interception and enhancing photosynthetic efficiency. Shoot architecture is defined by plant height, leaf morphology, and branching pattern, which are regulated by a complex network of plant hormones and environmental factors. Brassinosteroids (BRs) are among the classic plant hormones that regulate plant architecture. Here, we investigated the functions of Cabbage (Cbg) genes in maize which are orthologs of Arabidopsis CYP90A1/CPD and encode CYP90A, a key BR biosynthetic enzyme. Using reverse genetics, we identified and characterized cbg1 and cbg2 mutant alleles recovered from UniformMu transposon stocks. Our genetic mutant analysis indicated that Cabbage genes function collectively; each single mutant (cbg1 and cbg2) was indistinguishable from its wild-type siblings. In contrast, cbg1;cbg2 double mutants exhibited severe developmental defects including dwarf stature, fewer tassel branches, and smaller, erect leaves. These defects lead to shoots with tightly wrapped leaves forming a cabbage-like head that restricts inflorescence (tassel and ear) emergence and results in loss of fertility. Consistent with impaired BR biosynthesis, cbg1;cbg2 double mutants had significantly reduced levels of downstream BR metabolites. Treatment of wild-type and single mutant germinating seedlings with the BR biosynthetic inhibitor, Propiconazole (PCZ), phenocopied untreated cbg1;cbg2 double mutants, particularly in mesocotyl elongation. Supplementation with exogenous brassinolide (BL) alone was not adequate to restore mesocotyl elongation in the double mutants. These mutant phenotypes are consistent with impaired BR biosynthesis and demonstrate that Cabbage genes (Cbg1 and Cbg2) function redundantly to regulate plant development. Overall, these findings on Cabbage genes highlight the potential of BRs for crop improvement.

papers.title: Decomposing tissue-of-origin aging clocks reveals composite aging states across cancers
papers.abstract: Aging is accompanied by tissue-specific molecular remodeling, yet whether tumors retain or depart from these programs remains unclear. In a pan-cancer analysis we show that age-associated molecular changes in tumors are organized by tissue of origin and partially mirror matched normal tissue trends. We introduce tissue-of-origin aging clocks to measure each tumor's deviation from its expected tissue aging, and ClockSHAP to decompose deviations into pathway-level contributions. Across breast and five other cancers, this decomposition reveals composite aging states in which youth-like deviations in proliferative pathways coexist with older-like deviations in damage-response and signaling pathways. In breast cancer, a clock trained only on normal tissues, applied without retraining, reproduces its deviations and pathway structure in two independent cohorts (~9,700 tumors), aligns with molecular subtype and TP53 mutation status, and predicts survival. These findings show how cancers reshape tissue-of-origin aging programs and provide a framework for applying and interpreting aging clocks in disease.

papers.title: Force regulates mitotic entry timing during Drosophila gastrulation
papers.abstract: Cell division and cell shape changes drive tissue morphogenesis. Cell division is tightly regulated by biochemical factors that influence the cell cycle. Past work in our lab showed how contractility of mesoderm cells influences cell division orientation during Drosophila gastrulation. Whether contractile forces that drive morphogenetic folding influence the timing of coincident mitotic divisions is unknown. During Drosophila gastrulation, cell division is regulated by mitotic entry of cells in stereotypic regions across the embryo, termed mitotic domains. Here, we examine the role of morphogenesis in the timing of mitotic entry in the mitotic domains. To do this, we disrupted adherens junctions to globally disrupt force transmission across the embryo. In addition, we examined the timing of mitotic entry in mutants that affect mesoderm invagination. Our data suggests a role for mesoderm invagination in mitotic domain 1 timing.

papers.title: SH2 Domain Protein E sustains perivascular fibroblasts to maintain arterial stability
papers.abstract: Developing arteries must withstand pulsatile blood flow while remaining sufficiently flexible to accommodate changing hemodynamic demands. Endothelial interactions with perivascular cells and the extracellular matrix (ECM) are essential for this balance, but the signaling mechanisms that coordinate them remain incompletely understood. We previously showed that SH2 domain protein E (She), an endothelial adaptor protein implicated in ABL signaling, is required to maintain the size and structural stability of the dorsal aorta (DA) in zebrafish embryos. she mutant embryos develop DA collapse and circulatory failure at 4 to 5 days post-fertilization, yet the underlying cause has not been identified. Here, we investigated the role of She in recruiting ECM-producing perivascular stromal cells to regulate the structural stability of the DA. She mutants had fewer collagen producing perivascular stromal cells between the DA and posterior cardinal vein. This correlated with smaller perivascular col1a1 and col5a1 expression domains, reduced col1a1 transcript and Collagen I pro-peptide levels, and increased DA distensibility. Single-cell RNA sequencing independently identified a reduced relative abundance of a perivascular fibroblast subpopulation. In contrast, DA-associated mural cell number, laminin immunoreactivity, and local col4a1 transcript levels were not detectably altered. Partial ablation of mural cells alleviated DA narrowing and circulatory failure, while the nitric oxide donor sodium nitroprusside provided partial rescue. These findings support a contribution of mural cell-dependent vascular tone to the collapse of the mechanically vulnerable DA. Mutants also exhibited cardiac chamber enlargement, increased atrial and bulbus arteriosus deformation, atrioventricular regurgitation, and increased Elastin B accumulation in the enlarged bulbus arteriosus. However, endocardial-specific She expression failed to rescue circulatory failure, supporting its requirement in the vascular endothelium. Together, these findings argue that She functions in the vascular endothelium to recruit and/or maintain perivascular stromal cells, which produce fibrillar collagens required for arterial stability. These results reveal a new mechanism by which signals from the vascular endothelium promote ECM support to maintain arterial vascular stability.

papers.title: Conjugative delivery of a miniature Cas nuclease for broad range recipient gene editing
papers.abstract: Efficient delivery of the Cas endonuclease into target cells avoiding toxic effects remains one of the limiting steps of CRISPR-Cas gene editing technologies. Bacterial conjugation delivers protein and DNA directly into recipient bacteria, since the conjugative relaxase travels through a type IV secretion system covalently attached to the transferred DNA strand. We previously showed that fusion proteins relaxase- Cas12a or relaxase- base editor are translocated by conjugation and recover gRNA-guided nuclease or base-editing activity in recipient bacteria, despite the large size of the fusion. Aiming to improve the efficiency and to broaden the range of susceptible recipient bacteria, here we test translocation of the miniature type V-U4 nuclease Cas12n, fused to two unrelated conjugative relaxases, MobA and TrwC from RSF1010 and R388 respectively. Both fusions of 139 and 168 kDa were stably produced in Escherichia coli donor cells, mobilized their cognate plasmid as efficiently as the wild-type relaxases, and directed guide-dependent cleavage of a chromosomal target in the donor. Translocation and activity in recipient cells were tested with a lethality assay based on the loss of transconjugants viability caused by double-strand breaks introduced by the translocated nuclease. When MobA-Cas12n was delivered together with a mobilizable plasmid which encoded the guide RNA, conjugation frequency was reduced by more than one order of magnitude relative to both a non-targeting guide RNA and a nuclease-free relaxase control, indicating target-specific cleavage of the recipient chromosome. When assayed in parallel with previously characterized TrwC-Cas12a, MobA-Cas12n showed better protein yields and higher activity in recipient cells. This work extends the range of Cas proteins deliverable by conjugative relaxases to miniature nucleases. The fusion with relaxase MobA allows the use of the promiscuous RP4 conjugative system for conjugative delivery, extending the range of recipient bacteria potentially targeted by this tool.

papers.title: Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic analysis of oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid against extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producing Escherichia coli in an in vitro bladder infection model: impact on clinical breakpoints
papers.abstract: Uropathogens with acquired ESBL-genes can limit effective oral treatment options. Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid can be used as targeted therapy (500/125mg, 8-hourly). Despite favorable urinary pharmacokinetics (PK), there is little urine-specific data that quantifies the exposure required for bacterial clearance. A dynamic in vitro bladder model was employed, allowing for the simulated treatment of UTIs with oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. Sixteen Escherichia coli isolates (12 clinical ceftriaxone-resistant uropathogens, 4 laboratory isolates) were selected. Bacterial response to treatment, emergence of resistance, exposure-response targets and PK/PD indexes were explored. Following simulation of standard-dose oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (500/125mg, 8-hourly; Cmax 935mg/L; AUC0-24 14272mg/L), 14/16 isolates displayed no growth at the end of treatment, with elimination in seven isolates confirmed after a 24h antibiotic-free follow up. As exposure was reduced, greater survival and regrowth were observed. Only two isolates had significant post-exposure rises in MIC (32 to 128mg/L, 64 to 256mg/L). %T>MIC was the best predictor for end of treatment outcome (?log10cfu/mL: stasis 52.7%, 1log10 kill 61.8%, 2log10 kill 71.1%, R2=0.9062). Lower R2 values were found with EUCAST MIC measurements (fixed 2mg/L clavulanic acid) as compared to CLSI MIC measurements (2:1 amoxicillin to clavulanic acid). Monte Carlo simulations indicated that standard-dose 8-hourly would achieve all %T>MIC targets in >95% of virtual patients with MICs ?64 mg/L, regardless of MIC method (CLSI or EUCAST). Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid displays time-dependent killing against ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli. This data supports clinical breakpoints for uncomplicated UTI for isolates with MIC ? 64mg/L, assuming 500/125mg oral dosing 8-hourly.

papers.title: Benchmarking temporal causal discovery for fully and partially observed biochemical kinetic models
papers.abstract: Accurately reconstructing networks of biochemical reactions is a crucial yet unsolved problem for leveraging advances in experimental techniques that track intracellular dynamics in a time-resolved fashion. This task is further challenged by the fact that we typically observe only part of the system, while many variables shaping the dynamics remain unobserved. Causal discovery methods can infer causal relations from purely observational data and account for unobserved variables. They therefore hold promise for yielding faithful, mechanistically interpretable representations of underlying biochemical interactions, but their potential in this context remains underexplored. In this work, we provide a systematic benchmark of state-of-the-art temporal causal discovery methods (tMIIC, PCMCI+/LPCMCI and SVAR-FCI) on time-series data from simulations of biochemical kinetics of mass action and Michaelis-Menten type modelled as systems of nonlinear stochastic differential equations, including an experimentally calibrated model of the epidermal growth factor receptor signalling network. By selectively omitting data, we consider the problem of reconstructing these networks in the presence of both latent confounders and unobserved species participating in reactions. We find that tMIIC and PCMCI+/LPCMCI achieve the highest overall prediction quality, with tMIIC able to handle larger samples within the same runtime budget. We identify, as the main condition for optimal performance of causal discovery, the consistency between data-sampling regimes (sampling intervals, trajectory length) and the typical timescales of the system. We establish that causal discovery can detect latent confounders via bidirected edges and unobserved species via time-delayed edges, locating hidden effects and encoding information on their typical timescales, provided that the data sampling guarantees adequate temporal resolution. As such, our results can guide the choice of hyperparameters in causal discovery algorithms and of data-sampling regimes to optimize network-reconstruction performance.

papers.title: Genetic diversity, agroecosystems, and climate suitability of cacao in Panama: historical legacies and conservation priorities
papers.abstract: Theobroma cacao is a strategic resource for socioeconomic development and ancestral knowledge preservation in Panama. We integrated SNP genotyping, historical analysis, and climate suitability modeling to characterize the genetic resources of Panamanian cacao and inform future conservation priorities. We genotyped 153 cacao accessions from eight provinces using 96 SNP markers, assessed genetic diversity and ancestry composition, evaluated associations between ancestry and collection habitat (farms, forests, and home gardens), and projected current and future (2050, SSP5-8.5) climatic suitability using species distribution models. Genetic diversity was moderate (He = 0.384) with high admixture (54.7%); Amelonado (46.3%) and Criollo (29.1%) predominated. Criollo ancestry was strongly associated with home gardens and, to a lesser extent, forests, relative to farms (Firth-adjusted OR = 76.8, p < 0.001, and OR = 20.7, p = 0.013), whereas Amelonado predominated in commercial farms, reflecting pre-Columbian dispersal, colonial persistence, commercial introductions, and modern breeding. Climatically suitable area is projected to increase 11.9% by 2050 (8,780 to 9,825 km2), with gains in Chiriqu&iacute, Veraguas, and northwestern Dari&eacute, and losses along the Pacific coast of Veraguas and southwestern Los Santos. Human-managed agroecosystems, particularly home gardens, play a disproportionate role in maintaining Criollo-associated ancestry in Panama, including Criollo-associated genotypes not currently held in international reference collections. We recommend a national germplasm bank and the integration of genetic and climate information into conservation and adaptation strategies for Panamanian cacao.

papers.title: Development of Novel NPC1-Targeting Autophagy Inhibitors for the Treatment of Uveal Melanoma
papers.abstract: Background: Uveal melanoma (UM) is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, and up to 50% of patients develop liver metastases. Metastatic UM responds poorly to conventional chemotherapy and currently available immunotherapies, highlighting the need for new therapeutic strategies. Because UM cells rely on lysosome-dependent stress-response pathways, including autophagy, we evaluated previously reported betulinic acid (BetA) derivatives and identified ALS-997 as a potent inhibitor of autophagic flux in UM cells. Methods: The anticancer activity of BetA derivatives was evaluated using the NCI-60 cancer cell line panel and WST-1 viability assays in UM cell lines and normal human melanocytes. Effects on autophagy and lysosomal function were assessed by western blotting for mTOR and autophagy associated proteins, LysoTracker Green imaging, and filipin III/LAMP2 staining. Apoptosis was evaluated by PARP cleavage and caspase-3 cleavage. The interaction of ALS-997 with Niemann-Pick disease type C1 (NPC1) was examined using a cellular thermal shift assay and computational molecular docking. NPC1 expression in UM cells and normal melanocytes was compared by quatitative PCR and western blotting. Results: ALS-997 preferentially reduced the viability of UM cell relative to normal melanocytes. Treatment with ALS-997 disrupted autophagic flux and lysosomal function, induced lysosomal cholesterol accumulation, and activated apoptotic signaling. ALS-997 also altered the thermal stability of NPC1, supporting cellular target engagement, while molecular docking predicted a direct interaction between ALS-997 and NPC1. NPC1 expression was higher in UM cells than in normal melanocytes. Conclusions: ALS-997 is a BetA-derived compound that disrupts lysosomal cholesterol homeostasis and autophagic flux, leading to apoptosis in UM cells. These findings support NPC1 as a potential therapeutic target in UM.

papers.title: Human placental stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles ameliorate loss of intestinal stem cell subtypes in experimental necrotizing enterocolitis
papers.abstract: Background: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a devastating intestinal disease in premature infants with epithelial barrier disruption and loss of intestinal stem cells (ISCs). While depletion of active ISC (aISC) populations has been reported in NEC, the impact of NEC on reserve ISC (rISC) populations during early postnatal development remains poorly understood. We examined developmental and disease-associated changes in ISC subpopulations and evaluated the effects of human placental stem cell-derived extracellular vesicle (hPSC-EV) therapy on ISC preservation and recovery. Methods: Experimental NEC was induced in neonatal rat pups through exposure to NEC stressors with animals assigned as breastfed controls (BF), NEC, or NEC treated with hPSC-EVs (NEC-EV). Ileal tissue was assessed histologically and immunostained for SOX9, OLFM4, HOPX, BMI1, and Ki67. ISC populations were quantified across early postnatal development (32, 56, and 96 hours of life), during NEC progression, and with EV therapy. Results: NEC caused significant histological injury accompanied by marked reductions in SOX9+ and OLFM4+ cells, indicating early and sustained loss of aISC populations. Among rISC markers in established NEC, BMI1+ cells were preserved, whereas HOPX+ cells were significantly reduced. Assessment of healthy early postnatal development revealed that SOX9+ and OLFM4+ cell numbers remained relatively stable, while HOPX+ and BMI1+ populations significantly expanded and were predominantly proliferative. Early NEC did not initially deplete HOPX+ cells but prevented their normal developmental expansion, resulting in the observed reduction of HOPX+ cell abundance during established disease. Treatment with hPSC-EVs significantly improved intestinal architecture and restored SOX9+, OLFM4+, and HOPX+ cell populations to near-control levels. Conclusions: NEC differentially affects ISC subpopulations in the developing intestine, causing loss of aISC and disrupting the expansion of HOPX+ rISC. Preservation and restoration of both aISC and HOPX+ rISC populations may contribute to epithelial regeneration and recovery. These findings identify HOPX-associated development and regeneration as potential therapeutic targets and demonstrate that hPSC-derived extracellular vesicles support ISC recovery and intestinal repair in experimental NEC.

papers.title: Dynamic multi-omics analysis of Adenovirus-induced rAAV-producing stable cell lines reveals the interplay between adenoviral infection and host cell metabolism
papers.abstract: Recombinant adeno-associated viruses (rAAV) are invaluable delivery vehicles for gene therapy. However, to make rAAV-based therapies more accessible, there is a need to increase rAAV titers. Here we analyze the phenotypic variation among 30 Adenovirus-induced stably-transfected human producer cell clones to identify metabolic signatures associated with high vs low rAAV production. Exometabolomic characterization revealed decreased amino acid consumption in higher producers. Analysis of RNA-Seq data in the context of a genome-scale metabolic model identified upregulated carnosine biosynthesis-associated pathways during the first 6 hours post infection with adenovirus, relative to uninfected growth. Meanwhile, late infection timepoints exhibited increased amino acid release and de novo biosynthesis of serine, glycine, and arginine. Moreover, high producers decreased expression of genes linked with cholesterol biosynthesis and increased HMG-CoA degradation via HMGCL. Furthermore, sphingosine and ceramide biosynthesis genes were altered in high-producers in directions previously reported to resist cell death and suppress immune signaling. Overall, these findings elucidate the metabolic modulation upon adenoviral infection in a helper virus-induced AAV production process using stably transfected human cell lines.
